I gave a 45 minute presentation entitled “ Your Game Is A Harness” as part of Indie Rodeo in Calgary on 9/12/26. After speaking with a lot of people after my talk, I thought it would be good to more broadly share the ideas I presented there in a form that could be enjoyed by people beyond just those who attended the conference.

Also, because I talk about AI a lot on this blog, people assume I use AI to write. This is not true! Everything below is 100% human authored, with me writing the post with basically only the slides I presented as a reference (this is not a transcription). As much as I enjoy using AI to write code and tools, I get a similar enjoyment out of writing “ the old way”, especially as I have no reason to try and make any part of this process more efficient.

So with that all out of the way, I present to you my first ever blogification of a talk I gave. Enjoy!

## Introduction

[I give a small introduction to myself and my own work, that I’m omitting here, as you’re on my website]

I want to talk about using LLMs in game development. Not one-shot type demos that look cool on Twitter, but like real development. Where you’re working eight hours a day, 5 days a week, etc.

And before I get into it, I think it’s useful to level set about LLMs. Or at least get into some basics so the rest of what I talk about here makes sense. I recognize that for a lot of this people this will be review, so if you just want to get into the dev-loop stuff, scroll down to the next section.

My journey into using LLMs for dev work started with a moodboarding site I made called mood.site . This was pre “ agentic” anything, but I wanted to test and see if ChatGPT at the time could actually code anything. The process was a lot of me just blindly copy/pasting code into ChatGPT’s web interface. The process sucked, but I was surprised at the results. I built the site! It worked! I still needed to verify a fair amount of stuff myself, but it was enough to convert me. If I didn’t have access to an LLM I wouldn’t have been able to make that site happen in near the amount of time it ended up taking me (~2-3 weeks of nights, probably like 20 hours total). I’d probably still be working on building the first version today.

Since then, mood has become something of a testbed for me moving through LLM stuff (and a mildly successful project on its own!), and has inspired me to kick up lots of other projects that use similar stacks. Additionally, LLMs have gotten better, especially with things like Claude Code and later Claude models. From my own experience, I feel like now there is very little, if anything, I think an LLM can’t do when it comes to a web-based stack.

It could be easy to then say LLMs can do everything , as so much of software is web software. But whenever I tried to use an LLM on building a non-web game thing , it was this resounding takeaway:

## “ LLMs are Bad At Games”

Any time I tried to use an LLM for a game-y thing, it would fall over. Maybe this is my own bias. I’ve been a game programmer for nearly 15 years, I think I know how things work. I can sniff out “ bad” game code a mile away. But when it comes to Svelte web-apps, I’m decidedly less well versed and am inclined to think that whatever code the LLM produces is “ good”. Maybe it’s actually garbage. But there is reason to believe the Svelte and web-stack stuff is quality, in part due to the fact that there are LOTS of high quality web projects with their source available online. Comparatively for games, I imagine there are orders of magnitude less data to train on.

Not only this, but games have a lot of stuff in them that isn’t code. Games aren’t just about putting static images and text in a layout. There are tons of things in games that aren’t easily representable by code. AND then on top of that there is all the same text layout stuff of web, but only as a subset of the 100 other systems a game needs to handle.

This is part of the reason why a lot of people have been making games in Three.js — they can easily represent assets as plain boxy primitives and skip a lot of the asset generation/conforming work and processing normally required for games. As a result, a lot of that stuff is slop because it lacks any real authorial voice outside of whatever the LLM median is.

However, maybe they have a point.

A key idea of the one-shot Three.JS workflow (as well as LLMs proficiency at building web apps) is that everything is code. By having stuff as code, it’s very easy for an LLM to be able to reason about it, make changes, etc.

However for traditional games, this is not the case. Or at least the full story. Games obviously have code, but there is a lot of other stuff that is not code. This means that there are key components of games that are effectively opaque to an LLM . If your game then relies on the effective puppeting and transforming of that opaque stuff, then an LLM is going to fall over when trying to work on your game.

I think a lot of the gamedev community maybe gave LLMs a go a bit ago and ran directly into this. The “ LLMs are bad/not useful/etc.” sentiment (massive caveat here, just talking about capability specifically and not potential society-ending implications) came from running headfirst into these limitations.

This is to say that, structurally, LLMs are bad at reading games. At least in their default state.

## LLM Basics

Let’s talk more about why, and what we can do about it.

Any call/prompt to any LLM service breaks down into three basic components. A system prompt, an assistant prompt, and a user prompt:

System prompt: Generic text shared across all users of a service. This usually describes the basics of the LLM itself, with something like “ You are Opus 5, an intelligent Large Language Model created by Anthropic…”. This isn’t to say these aren’t important (they are), but more that they aren’t super-relevant to our use case. You can see some examples of posted (and exfiltrated) system prompts for models here .

Assistant prompt: This is kind of a sidecar prompt section meant to help guide the AI in terms of what it is responding to. You can think of it basically as the model’s basic “ interaction” vector with your prompt, and represents something like the model’s “ response” to the user based on some input. You usually do not have to think about this.

User Prompt : This is really The Thing. Most any input you put into any AI tool goes here. Any submitted chat, code, etc. gets dumped into this section. When people talk about “ context”, they are largely talking about “ how many tokens are stored in the user (and assistant) portion of a prompt”.

It may be easy to think that each chat is a “ fresh” version of the above, but what actually happens is that, as you work with a model in a given session (the bounds of “ session” vary based on what service you are using — this can be a single Claude Code session before closing it, a “ chat” accessible in the side panel of a web hosted model, etc.), every prior message you sent to the model is re-submitted every time you send a message. It’s kind of like playing the old playground game where, on your turn, you have to say everyone else’s thing again before then adding your own thing for the next person to have to add on.

## Context and Context Pollution

As you do this over and over, you build up the “ context” of the session you’re working in.

This is all well and good, but a key thing to notice here is that you only really are able to address the “ latest” thing in your context (i.e., you submit a new message). Things from previous messages get submitted over and over again to the model. Hence, you want to make sure what’s in your context is “ good”, otherwise you can find yourself in degenerate scenarios where your context becomes polluted due to “ bad” things earlier continually informing new work.

Managing context then is a key thing in working with LLMs, and a new engineering practice called “ context engineering” has emerged in light of these constraints. Context engineering asks “ how can we get the best information into the context, with as little pollution as possible”.

There is a great blog post here on “ ways long contexts fail” that goes a bit more into this, but I’ll highlight the key part here:

Context Engineering itself is a really big topic that is outside the scope of this talk/blog, but we will be using some of the tenets of it here to explore how to help LLMs do a better job working with games.

Said differently, getting LLMs to work well with games is a context problem, not something that is intrinsically linked to how games or LLMs “ are” (or “ aren’t”!).

The complicating factor here though is, games are weird . Or at least: we have no real template to build a game. We have game engines, but there is effectively 0 standardized tooling for anything, in part because every game manifests its own needs differently from one another.

This is acutely unique to games (imo), but it manifests enough in other technological domains that a new concept has emerged in order to get agents to effectively “ work” with whatever your work product is: Harnesses.

## Some Description of the Idea of a Harness

The general idea of a Harness is that it’s some set patterns of actions an agent is meant to take in response to some well (or loosely) defined expected input. You’re probably already using a harness like Claude Code, but these can be augmented, extended, distilled, abstracted, etc. to better support the specific work you are trying to do. There’s also been a LOT of action in this space recently, with many harnesses being built for developing all sorts of things:

The key things these are all pointing to is: “ how can I better understand what I’m building, and guide that process as it is developed”. Harnesses can tie in things like iterating with a browser, telemetry, profiling, and even full SDLC work like making tickets, documents, etc.

However, the thing none of these do well is actually talk to your game. Your game is a bit of a black box, and most of what’s visible to an LLM is only the code-as-written, which as we talked about before, isn’t really enough. We know LLMs are already good at working with code, so it’s not like some harness itself solves that “ games aren’t just code” issue we ran into in the first place.

What really needs to happen here is that we can take all the stuff in games, and try to turn it into something the LLM is able to work with. We need to crack open the black box of your game and make more of it addressable directly by an LLM .

# Let’s Make a Game Legible To AI Agents

Here’s some very tangible, actionable things you can do for your game to make it more legible and workable by an LLM .

As a brief aside before getting started, it’s also worth noting here that a lot of these tips are good for game development in general . They get supercharged a bit with AI , but doing any of this will likely make working on your own games generally just better .

## Fixed Randomness

A running theme through this whole talk/post is the concept of determinism . Basically, how accurately can you reproduce a very specific state in your game. The general goal is that it should be very easy, and very exact. Doing this at the very end of your production will be VERY hard to do, and would likely require fundamental changes to your game in the 11th hour.

Instead, if you assume this constraint before you write your first line of code, and stick to it as a goal, you’ll be paving the path to a much more productive end game and not find yourself fighting off entropy and spaghetti code.

Something on my mind a lot recently is this scene from the first episode of Westworld:

I remember watching this when it came out thinking that it was so unrealistic as to be comedic. I very distinctly remember thinking “ Any complicated AI being would no be able to be debugged just by talking to it. That’s so dumb, you would obviously need actual real debugging tools. You’d be writing code, etc. Stupid!”

10 years on, now I’m not so sure.

Right now, there are two(-ish) groups of people that use AI . There are the default chat-interface people we’ll call Group A that use whatever OpenAI or Anthropic serves them in a web UI , and then there are the agent/harness people using things like Claude Code or Codex or Pi or whatever. Let’s call them Group B.

There is a tacit assumption right now that, like most all technology before, expertise and mastery (or a desire for it) drives a portion of Group A to Group B. You could call group B “ Expert Users”.

However, model advances seem to upset this status quo, advancing at a rate that seems to actually push Group B people back to Group A, as Group A’s default case gets stronger , and the mastery Group B developed is subsumed by the advances as to render them useless. Model enhancements seem to obviate the need for previously required workflows that were used to get better agent behavior .

For example — when I ask Claude to look for something, I do not tell it explicitly to search the web. However, it does search the web, as it knows broadly what I want based on what I asked it.

When I say “ I” here, I mean not only literally me-the-person, but also anything an agent may have access to: my computer documents, memory files, browsing history etc. When I ask an agent a question, I’m asking it with my whole visible-to-claude self.

Because of this, the model already does a really good job doing the thing I asked it to do. It has my previous context, it’s own memory on my computer, project context, etc.

And this is obviously not just me, but any version of an “ I” here, meaning this same capability is available to anyone else. I maintain that the best way to work with the AI is to just ask it stuff , so people that continue to just ask the model things are able to leverage all the AI advances without needing to really do anything extra. It just works.

“ Just ask it things” seems to be the only strategy that scales, and is immediately available to both expert and novice users equally. The asking here can be specific or well informed (think scientific/medical research, etc.), but the doing of the model increasingly becomes unrelated to the input, or more that it knows how to do what you ask of it, regardless of what you ask.

This stands apart from “ expert AI use advice” by presumably AI-use experts of the last few years, with much of it geared towards trying to coax the model to behave in a certain way. In fact, I think the idea of getting the model to “ perform” (i.e,, an expert’s work) is just becoming so much less of a thing because of model advances.

Karpathy recently talked about AI-use cohorts, and described the general “ expert” cohort like this :

> Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math & code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries… This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.

Notice of the passiveness of the word “ see” here. I don’t think this is a knowing wink to what I’m saying by him, but I think the idea of “ witnessing” is a similar dynamic to what I’m describing.

He goes on to talk about a higher tier of use that is even further divorced from model use, and is characterized almost solely by model access :

> And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work.

This is all to say that someone’s ability to leverage a model for some outcome seems to pale in comparison to simply having access to a great model that you can just ask things of that will do what you want. And knowing what to ask is not about model-use skill, but more about knowledge of the domain you’re asking the model about.

I think of it like this: Imagine there is some spectrum of “ all possible intelligence”, with the dumbest things on the left, and universe-understanding-at-atomic-level on the right (some may call this “ God”):

An interesting thing here is that we don’t really know where humans are compared to all possible intelligence, in part because we don’t really know what the upper bound of “ understanding” can be. If someone happens to know everything about our reality and Earth, they would be very smart based on our current frame of reference. But what if it turns out there are in fact many realities and many millions of Earth-like planets? That one being/person could be aptly described as dumb with a frame of reference that encompasses everything.

I think for our own sanity though, let’s assume that humans as is are in the middle of the pack:

If we assume that million-worlds-knower is on the graph, but not as intelligent as the Godhead, they may go somewhere here:

Now, let’s imagine the smartest possible human. Someone who intimately knows everything there is to know about everything we know we can know now, with immense ability for taking in new knowledge. Lets also imagine this “ smartest human” is The Best Human Person With AI . They know every possible way to interact with a model to get a good result, etc.

Combined, that’s almost certainly more the actual smartest person now, but no where near the million-worlds-knower. The “ smartest possible human” barely registers as any movement on the X-axis:

Compared to the span of all possible intelligence, our smartest human isn’t even close.

Now, let’s imagine that, the further you go to the right on the X axis, by definition your ability to know and reason about intelligences to the left of you grows exponentially the further you are from it. Said differently, a Godhead can understand inert matter more than the inert matter can understand itself. Inert matter has no ability to understand or conceive of a Godhead.

That is the extreme example, but imagine how this works with a sufficiently advanced AI . We already know, based on benchmarks, that a frontier model’s general intelligence is greater than any human in terms of it’s workable knowledge (and maybe intelligence as well, given the recently published math results from OpenAI ). Not only this, but our ability to reason about how LLMs now work is also far from a given, spawning a discipline in an of itself ( Interpretability ).

This puts LLMs now likely to the right of us. Tack on the compounding advances of a few years, maybe reaching superintelligence, and I suspect a sufficiently advanced AI would be probably about half way between us and the million-worlds-knower (I suspect that the limits of available compute, even at planetary scale, prevents AI from becoming God. For now).

It follows then, from my coarse, pseudoscientific diatribe, that a superintelligent AI would be able to understand what any human wants when it interacts with it. Or if not that, at least infinitely able to better understand the intention of what a human is asking of it.

Going back to that sense of an “ I” being your sort-of “ personal metadata”, a sufficiently advanced intelligence will be able to rapidly build up a picture of you, your needs, desires, preferences, etc., and serve you what you are looking for no matter how you ask it .

This is the “ seeing” of the Karpathy quote from above. We experience our desired action , no matter our input. AI-use “ Experts” have no leg to stand on.

This position puts me a bit at odds with this (popular) recent post . Its conclusion is:

> The useful distinction is between wielding an instrument with skill and delegating work without adequate understanding or oversight. That distinction applies to AI , and it gives us something more practical than declaring that an entire class of software cannot be a tool.

The author spends most of the post rebuking Rich Hickey’s talk about AI , which I think is correct, but the conclusion here I think is missing that the understanding -ness of use doesn’t have to implicitly come from the human. Or assuming that the human using the tool is implicitly the one that best-positioned to know how their own problem should be solved (or what approach should be taken). Or if nothing else should be expected to instruct the AI how to do the task asked of it.

Given what I talked about above, I just don’t think this is the case, or if it is, it will not be for much longer. The skill feels, to me, that it will be irrelevant in short order.

What will still matter is asking the right questions, informed by a problem space, etc. This sketches at notions of “ taste” that I think others have echoed as still relevant in the future, and I agree here.

I talk to people at work frequently about the idea of “ AI model advancements” as something like “ buy the index” investment advice. There was an industry wide push for putting SKILL.md files in repos about 8 months ago, to help models better understand codebases. I’m not sure this matters anymore, or more that “ making the tool itself be more AI-legible ” outperforms skills for evals, when benched against later models that are just simply better at figuring out what to do based on the default data they are given. “ Just ask the [better] model things”, like buying the index, is just incredibly hard to consistently beat.

To be clear, and to wrap this up, I don’t think this is necessarily a bad thing. I think a lot of the crazy harness engineering stuff of the last few years has been fun to watch but also a lot of noise. I get a lot of use out of AI by having a relatively “ dumb” process, and I find that I never run into token spend issues, reasoning loops, etc., and consistently get good results. I may even call myself an AI Expert (for now). But I would characterize this less about knowing individual tool use things, and more just an openness to try stuff, and follow my own taste to what I think is good. I care less and less about my meta-interactions with AI , and instead try to work on the paved path of just asking it things. If something doesn’t work, I just ask it again (which scales — I can ask an AI model something 1000x times and then sort through the produced solutions myself. The asking is trivially easy to automate!).

And my hope is that, as the walls to “ expert” use continue to be torn down, others can see these same benefits. Naïve uses becoming the “ best” way to use AI is actually the success outcome here. If good results from AI requires people to be well-versed in various tools and techniques, it undermines AI as a good solution as it puts up knowledge prerequisites for engagement. If instead people can get amazing results with little upfront work, that’s great! It democratizes the benefits of AI to people who don’t read all the blogs, Github repos, Karpathy posts, etc. It allows everyone to get the best possible output from a model. Everyone can be an expert.
